Florence, September. Tonight is "Researchers' Night", and Pietro has to present, together with Karl and Professor Innocenti, the story of the T, the Madonna and the river. It's his first presentation in front of a hundred people. He rehearses with Karl in the workshop.
So… Good evening. I'm Pietro and today we're talking about the T.
Too fast. First of all thank the organisers. Then present the structure: what you'll talk about, in what order.
"First of all I'd like to thank the organisers. My talk is divided into three parts: the T, the Madonna and the river."
Perfect. And when you change part?
"Let's move on now to the second part." And for the humidity graph?
You explain the axes first, then the curve. "On the horizontal axis are the months, on the vertical one the humidity. As you can see, the curve peaks in August."
And if I give a piece of data, do I have to say where it comes from?
Always. "According to Dr Camilleri's data…", "As emerges from Professor Ruggeri's report…". Data without a source is an opinion.
And if someone asks me a question I can't answer?
You say: "Good question. I'm not able to answer with certainty. I'll have to check." Nobody's going to eat you.
"To conclude…" and a single sentence, the one you want them to remember. You've got a notebook full of them.

Tre storie e una domanda

The European Researchers' Night was held every year on the last Friday in September, in hundreds of cities across Europe at the same time. In Florence, that year, the university had chosen as its venue the great cloister of Santa Maria Novella, lit by coloured lamps, with dozens of stands where researchers explained their work to the public: robots playing chess, microscopes trained on drops of Arno water, a PhD student handing out tastes of bread made from ancient wheat. And in the chapter house, the one with the fourteenth-century frescoes, at nine in the evening there was a talk with a title that had made many people curious: "Three stories and a question: the T, the Madonna and the river". There were three speakers: Professor Marta Innocenti, hydraulic engineer; Karl Borg, restorer; and Pietro, secondary-school pupil, fifteen.

The idea had been Professor Innocenti's. After the night of the alert, in May, she had kept in touch with Pietro, who emailed her every time he read something about rivers and didn't understand it. In July she had come to the church of San Leonardo to see the two Madonnas. At the end of August she had proposed to the university that a talk at Researchers' Night be devoted to what she called "the science of questions". "Three different stories," she had written to the organisers, "a painting, a panel, a river. But the same method: observe, make hypotheses, verify, decide. And the same boy asking the questions." The organisers had accepted at once. Pietro, when he heard, hadn't slept for three nights.

The problem was that Pietro had never spoken in front of a hundred people. He had done the debate tournament, of course, but there there were rules, opponents, a timer. Here there was only him, a screen and an audience of strangers, including, so the programme said, the rector of the university. For two weeks he rehearsed every evening in the workshop, with Karl acting as audience and coach. Karl taught him everything Ruggeri had taught him in Rome: announce the structure at the beginning, always say where a piece of data comes from, explain a graph's axes before the curve, never read the slides, look people in the eye, one at a time. "And if they ask you a difficult question," he told him, "don't make things up. Ever. It's the only rule that really counts."

Davide prepared the slides. Or rather, he drew them. He flatly refused to use ready-made computer images, and for two weeks spent every afternoon drawing by hand, with coloured pencils and watercolours, twenty-two plates that Karl then scanned one by one. There was Caravaggio's Beheading with the little T circled. There was an enlarged finger with the ridges of the print. There was a cross-section of the San Leonardo panel with the tree rings, counted one by one. There was the Arno in flood seen from the Ponte Vecchio, and next to it the same Arno dried up near Pisa. And there was, at the end, a drawing Davide refused to show anyone before the evening. "It's for the final sentence," was all he said. "Pietro knows which one."

The dress rehearsal took place at the trattoria, on Thursday evening, in front of an audience Pietro knew only too well: Graziella, Bellini, Guido the shoemaker, the fruit seller, two American tourists who didn't understand a word, and Lupino. Graziella took Mancini's kitchen tomato timer and set it for fifteen minutes. Pietro spoke for nineteen. When the tomato rang, halfway through the second part, Graziella raised a hand like a referee. "Too long," she said. "And you talk like a professor. Nobody listens to you if you talk like a professor. Talk like someone telling a story at dinner." Bellini, from his table, nodded. "Your grandmother's right," he said. "Data is for convincing professors. Stories are for convincing everyone else. You have to do both." Pietro cut four minutes that very night. Above all he cut the difficult words.

On Friday evening, the chapter house was fuller than it had been for years. The chairs ran out at half past eight, and people sat on the floor, on the steps, even on the window sills. In the front row was everyone. Graziella, in her coat for great occasions and, Pietro was sure, with a thermos labelled "herbal tea". Matei and Giulia with Viola, who had been five for four months and had asked to sit "next to the Madonna", that is next to the fresco. Bellini with his stick. Chiara. Davide with his mother Rita and his grandfather Efisio. Valeria, in her official capacity, with her councillor's sash. And next to them, someone Pietro hadn't expected: Signora Nunzia, ninety-two, who hadn't been to Florence for forty years and whom don Paolo had brought on the train specially.

The first talk was Karl's, about the T. He was excellent: calm, precise, with his Maltese accent that made even technical words sound musical. He explained X-ray fluorescence, the fingerprint, the ridges four tenths of a millimetre apart. "As emerges from Professor Ruggeri's report," he said, "the data is compatible with a child's finger. Compatible. Not proven." And he pointed out, in the third row, Professor Ruggeri in person, who had come from Rome and raised a hand to greet the audience, a little embarrassed. Then it was Professor Innocenti's turn; she spoke about the Arno, the May night, the retention basins, climate change. She showed a graph, drawn by Davide, with the rainfall of the last fifty years, and the curve rising, rising, rising.

Then it was Pietro's turn. He stood up, went to the lectern and for one long, terrible second couldn't say anything. He looked at the audience: a hundred unknown faces, the light of the lamps, the fourteenth-century frescoes on the walls. He felt his heart beating in his ears. Then he saw, in the front row, Graziella giving him a little nod, the same one she gave him when he was small and had to recite a poem at Christmas. And next to her Signora Nunzia, with her hands clasped on her stick, looking at him the way you look at a grandson. Pietro breathed. "First of all," he said, and his voice came out steadier than he expected, "I'd like to thank the organisers. And I'd like to thank someone who is here tonight and who, without knowing it, did the most important experiment in this whole story. Her name is Nunzia, and she is ninety-two."

The audience turned towards the front row, and Signora Nunzia, who hadn't expected anything of the kind, blushed like a girl. There was spontaneous applause. Pietro waited for it to finish, as Bellini had taught him, and then began. "My talk is divided into three parts," he said. "In the first I'll tell you a legend. In the second I'll show you how science verified it. In the third I'll tell you why, in the end, it wasn't science that decided." He told the story of the Madonna with two faces, Nunzia's grandmother, "in the time of the French". Then he moved on to the second part. He showed Davide's slide with the tree rings. "According to Dr Lapini's analyses," he said, "the tree was felled between 1318 and 1330. It's like reading a tree's diary." In the third row, Dr Lapini laughed and nodded.

Then Pietro showed a graph. It was the only graph in his part, and he had rehearsed it twenty times. "On the horizontal axis," he explained, "are the Saturdays of the open worksite, from June to September. On the vertical one, the number of visitors." He pointed to the curve. "As you can see, on the first Saturday there were seventeen. The curve rises slowly until July, then grows quickly, and peaks on the first Saturday in September: two hundred and ten people. The day we showed the digital reconstruction." He paused. "But the most important figure isn't in this graph. It's another number, which don Paolo gave me. At Sunday Mass, at Easter, there were twelve people. Now, usually, there are fifty. And the curve, says don Paolo, has levelled off."

Then came the third part, the one Pietro feared most, because there were no data, only a choice. "Let's move on now to the third part," he said. "The hardest." He told them about the dilemma: remove the eighteenth century to see the fourteenth, or leave it. He told them about the assembly in the church, the sixty-eight parishioners, the young farmer and the retired schoolteacher. And then he told them what Signora Nunzia had said: that the eighteenth-century painter had covered the face of sorrow so that people wouldn't cry, and that she wanted to see the old one just once, without losing the other. "Science," said Pietro, "told us what was underneath. But it couldn't tell us what to do. That was decided by the people who pray to that Madonna. I'd like to dwell on this point, because in my opinion it's the most important of the whole evening."

"In the first story," he continued, "the T, we found a piece of data, and we stopped there, because we couldn't go further without making things up. In the second, the river, we used science to prevent a tragedy from happening again. In the third, the Madonna, we used science to understand, and then we set it aside to decide. They're three different uses of the same thing. But in all three there was someone asking questions, and someone with the patience to answer. Professor Ruggeri. Professor Innocenti. Karl. Chiara. Don Paolo. My grandmother, who taught me always to ask about the grandchildren." The audience laughed. Graziella, in the front row, covered her face with her hands.

Then came the questions. The first was from a biology student, who asked whether the T could be studied using DNA. Karl replied that no, unfortunately: after four hundred years, and with the restorations, nothing analysable remained. The second was from an elderly gentleman, who asked Professor Innocenti whether Florence would still be safe in fifty years. She answered honestly: "I'm not able to say with certainty. It depends on what we do now. According to the climate models, extreme rainfall will increase. The retention basins help, but they're not enough. Everything else is needed: less concrete, more trees, more attention." The gentleman nodded. It was the old man from via dei Serragli, the one Pietro had persuaded to leave his home. He stood up and shook the professor's hand. Then, passing the lectern, he shook Pietro's too.

Then a journalist from a Milan weekly stood up, the same one who two years earlier had put the T circled in red on the cover. He asked, with a slightly sly smile, whether in the end it could be said that the T was the signature of Totò, Caravaggio's secret child. Silence fell in the hall. Karl answered calmly, as he had all evening. "According to the data, the print is compatible with a child's finger. From what emerges from the hospital register, in 1608 in Malta there was a seven-year-old boy called Salvatore. But no data links the two things. We can't say it." The journalist insisted: and if he had to bet? It was Pietro who answered. "We leave bets to novelists," he said. "We can only say what we know. The name, if there is one, is known only to that child." The journalist laughed and sat down. The next day, in his article, he quoted the sentence word for word.

The third question came from Viola. Nobody expected it. She stood up on her chair, before Giulia could stop her, and asked in her high voice, which could be heard at the back of the hall: "But the old Madonna's hand, what is it pointing at?" There was a moment's silence, then a general, affectionate laugh. Pietro looked at Viola, then at the audience. It was the question he couldn't answer. The one with the question mark as big as a page, in the black notebook. He could have made something up: the founders' tomb, a legend, a symbol. The audience wouldn't have noticed. But he looked at Karl, and remembered the only rule that really counted. "Good question," he said. "I'm not able to answer with certainty. I have a hypothesis, but I haven't verified it yet. I'll have to check. And I'll let you know."

In the third row, Professor Ruggeri began to applaud. On his own, for a few seconds, while the others didn't quite understand why. Then he stood up. "Excuse me," he said to the moderator, "may I add something?" The moderator nodded. "In thirty years of conferences," said Ruggeri, "I've heard hundreds of speakers, many more famous than this boy. Almost none of them has ever answered a question by saying 'I don't know'. It's the hardest answer, and the most scientific. This boy gave it to a five-year-old girl, in front of a hundred people, when he could have made up anything." He turned to Pietro. "At your age, I would have made something up." Then he sat down again. The audience applauded for a long time, and this time everyone knew why.

Only the final sentence was missing. Pietro asked Karl to show the last slide, the one Davide hadn't wanted to show anyone. On the screen appeared a watercolour: a long table, seen from above, and around the table many people, each holding an object. An old man with a tiny brush. A woman with a ladle. A boy with a black notebook. A man with a shovel. An elderly lady with a stick. A professor with a magnifying glass. A little girl raising her hand. In the middle of the table, a steaming pot of ribollita. And above, at the top, a single word written in capitals: "WHY?". Pietro looked at the drawing, then at the audience. "To conclude," he said, "I'd like to tell you the most important sentence I've learned this year. It isn't mine. It's Ruggeri's. 'The questions that are not strictly necessary are the ones that lead to discoveries.' Thank you for your attention."

After the talk, in the lit cloister, there was a small improvised party. Graziella opened the "herbal tea" thermos, which of course contained ribollita, and offered it to the rector of the university, who took three little plastic cups and asked for the recipe. Graziella told him he could have ninety-eight per cent. Signora Nunzia, sitting on a bench under the arcades, received a queue of people who wanted to meet her, like a queen. Efisio and don Paolo discovered they had been born in the same year and began arguing about which of them remembered 1966 better. Davide was surrounded by a group of Fine Arts students who wanted to know who had taught him to draw like that. "A retired restorer," he replied. "And a river."

Ruggeri went up to Karl and told him something that Karl told everyone that evening at least ten times. The scientific article on the T, which Ruggeri was writing for an international journal, would be signed by two authors: Ruggeri and Borg. "Your name comes second," said the professor, "but only in reverse alphabetical order. And in the acknowledgements there's Pietro, with his not strictly necessary questions." Karl was speechless. Then he asked him the question that had been tormenting him for months: whether after his degree he should go back to Rome or stay in Florence. Ruggeri looked at him, then at the cloister, the party, Graziella with her thermos, Davide with the students. "Karl," he said, "Rome has the books. Here there are the questions. I would stay here. And I'm not saying it out of politeness."

Karl phoned his mother at about half past eleven, from the cloister, even though in Malta it was the same time and she had been asleep for a while. Mrs Borg answered on the third ring, worried, convinced something had happened. Karl told her everything in Maltese, so fast that she had to ask him three times to repeat it: the talk, the article with his name, Ruggeri's advice. Then he told her, his voice trembling a little, that he might stay in Florence even after his degree. There was a long silence at the other end. Karl thought his mother was sad. Instead she said only, in Italian, with the accent of the village priest who had taught her the formulas: "Dear son, I look forward to hearing from you. But come home for Christmas." Karl laughed until he cried, sitting alone on the cloister step.

It was almost midnight when Pietro finally managed to sit down, alone, on a step of the cloister, with a glass of orange juice in his hand and his head spinning. Professor Innocenti sat down next to him. For a while they looked at the coloured lamps without saying anything. Then she took a folded sheet out of her bag and gave it to him. It was a letter from the university, on headed paper, signed by the rector. It said that every summer the university organised a school for secondary-school pupils passionate about science, two weeks of labs, lessons, excursions, and that for the following summer a place was reserved for "the young speaker at Researchers' Night". Pietro read the letter twice. "I still don't know what I want to do when I grow up," he said quietly. "Art history, science, journalism…" The professor smiled. "Good," she said. "It means you keep asking yourself questions."

Walking home, across the Ponte alla Carraia, the family scattered in small groups along the river. The Arno, that night, was calm and dark, and reflected the lights of the embankments like a mirror. Viola was asleep in Matei's arms. Graziella walked arm in arm with Signora Nunzia, who would sleep at her place, in the guest room above the trattoria, before going back to San Leonardo the next day. The two women talked in low voices about recipes, grandchildren and dead husbands, as if they had known each other for ever. Halfway across the bridge, Signora Nunzia stopped and looked at the river. "My grandmother said the Arno is a person," she said. "A bit good and a bit bad. Like everyone." Graziella nodded. "Mine too," she said. "But she also said you just have to feed it."

That night, in the black notebook, Pietro didn't write a summary. He stuck in the rector's letter and, below it, the photograph Mancini had taken during the talk: him at the lectern, with Davide's slide behind him, and in the front row Signora Nunzia and Graziella, blurred, smiling. Then he opened the page with the question mark as big as a page, the one about the Madonna's hand, and wrote underneath, in small letters: "Promised to Viola: to verify." And further down, after thinking about it for a long time, he added a sentence, the last of the evening, the one he hadn't said to the audience but wanted to remember: "Today I said 'I don't know' in front of a hundred people. It was the hardest thing I've ever done. And it's the thing I'm proudest of."
